292.t: Daughter Ione's band and her love of dancing
292.s: Ione played piano in a five-piece band before marrying at 16; her grandson and Donald and dancing.
292.ch: Courtship, family and the French Quarter
292.q: Well, I don't remember if we had them anymore or not after that. We mostly relied on the piano after that and the phonograph. Because everyone played music. And then sometimes I own and her band would come. They'd have a sax in there and a cornet, a drum, a piano. I think they had about a…

742.t: His father Moose Charlap, Peter Pan songs, and a house full of songwriters
742.s: His father wrote most of the Peter Pan music and died when Bill was six or seven; songwriters visited the house, and his own daughters now meet musicians unawares.
742.q: like “I’m Flying,” “I’ve Gotta Crow,” “Tender Shepherd,” “I Won’t Grow Up,” that’s all my dad, as many pop songs such as “I Was Telling Her About You,” you might know that one, Joe Williams did that, Betty Carter used to sing it I hear. And many others. He died when I was quite young, I was six or…

985.t: Artistic parents: playwright father, opera-singer mother, home cabarets
985.s: Evans describes his father the playwright and professor, his mother the opera singer, home cabarets, their divorce, and siblings.
985.q: Well first, my father was a playwright and a full time teacher teaching African-American studies for 35 years. He taught at Princeton, taught at Trenton State, and taught at Rutgers, one of the reasons I went to Rutgers. He wasn’t there when I went there but that’s one of the reasons. So that, I…

593.t: His mother, Frances Sweeney and Ben Webster ballads
593.s: His mother could not understand his jazz; after Frances Sweeney died he played Ben Webster ballads repeatedly.
593.q: She couldn’t understand it. She said it all sounds the same, this jazz. And I remember when Frances Sweeney, who is prominent in the book, died, the only way I could get some kind of consolation was to play Ben Webster ballads again and again and again. And I almost drove my mother crazy.

960.t: Musical families in New Orleans and Jordan's parents
960.s: Music as a fulcrum of New Orleans families; his mother's family of 16, his father's Crowley roots, and Alvin Batiste introducing his parents.
960.q: That’s an interesting analogy. I’ve never really thought of it that way. You know I guess in certain areas of the country where certain livelihoods or occupations would dominate, and obviously in New Orleans the music has always been a dominant influence in terms of our culture. And I think that’s…

684.t: Parents, sister Nicki and a musical home
684.s: Her parents adjusting to both daughters moving to the US; non-musical but music-loving parents, classical lessons on clarinet and flute.
684.q: Exactly. I’m the older sister so it’s my fault obviously. And both Nicki and I came sort of a year apart. We both got grants from the Australian government to do some private study here. So we actually came separately. And oh my gosh, it’s been a massive adjustment I have to say, for Mom and Dad.…

661.s: She recalls her father practicing piano, always dressed up, making home movies including Armstrong footage, and her Panamanian upbringing.
661.q: Yeah. I mean I remember him then because my memory was that — one of them was that he would practice. Sit at a piano and practice classical music. And then the other one, the other two is that he was always dressed up in the house. He never walked around the house in a bathrobe or slippers or…

549.t: Parents, school music, trumpet and cousin Dick Schaap
549.s: His mother's violin demand, the school music program, his memory, and cousin Dick Schaap's tickets and Billy Crystal ties.
549.q: Yes. No. My mother was eventually thrilled. She was fighting the sports and music thing. I mean her idea was — I wanted to learn an instrument and it was violin or nothing so I said nothing.

550.s: His mother was a ballet teacher; no musicians in the family.
550.q: My mom was a dancer, a ballet dancer. She had a dancing school, a dance academy on Long Island. My father is not, you know, they’re not musicians. And we wonder about that. I mean I really don’t know where that came from. It was just, I don’t know. I guess it’s a blessing and a curse. Well I really…

531.t: Grandfather, parents and father conducting the Vienna Philharmonic
531.s: Her mother was her early musical guide; her father, a retired forest ranger, air-conducted with headphones, impressing her deeply.
531.q: My father is still alive. He’s actually turning 86 tomorrow and he’s still going strong. We actually still go hiking together a lot. My mother, unfortunately she passed away in 2016 but she really has been my musical guide early in my life. She was a music teacher and she was the one who got me…

672.t: Parents who were not show business people
672.s: Her family never pushed; music was around her from childhood.
672.ch: Coming to New York and signing
672.q: And I was blessed here again. My people were not show business people. They did not push. They wouldn’t have known how. It was, the music was in my face, all the, from the time I was a little kid.

680.t: His non-musician father and the family vaudeville show
680.s: His father could comp chords, the family put on an hour-long show, and Burton later discovers both parents had played in high-school bands.
680.q: he was an inspiring non-musician. He was the reason we all had music lessons. He grew up during the Depression. His father was an itinerant preacher. They never had money for instruments or that sort of thing, although he did manage to...somewhere around high school he managed to get a trumpet and…

508.t: Family pressure to practice and his father's uncomplaining example
508.s: His mother, Wynton and his father nagged him to practice; he admired his father for never complaining about playing an unpopular music, unlike New York musicians.
508.q: My dad was more of an influence just because he just…. I mean he would…. They would all get on my ass about not practicing and not being serious.

100.t: To Denmark, and Alban Berg in Vienna memories
100.s: Travelling to Denmark with his grandmother, the dying great-grandmother, and his fond memories of Alban Berg, the coffee houses and early phonograph and violin.
100.q: the Nazis were taking over all these bureaucratic positions and didn’t know anything, so she managed to talk them into giving her a Danish passport. The Danish consulate was cooperative, I guess. She dumped me at my grandmother’s place and went to Denmark and prepared things there. Then my…
